name: Appearance and Physical Modeling
text:
# Appearance and Physical Modeling
## Overview
Appearance and Physical Modeling extends the standard [3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)](#1174-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs.md) representation to support [physically based rendering](#6815-physically-based-rendering-pbr-lighting.md) (PBR), relighting, and volumetric light transport, solving the limitations of base 3DGS which relies on fixed Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients that cannot accurately represent complex specularities, dynamic lighting, or non-vacuum media [G]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Gaussian Representation and Truncation](12855-gaussian-representation-and-truncation.md) by focusing on the radiance and material representation rather than geometric simplification, and distinguishes itself from [Physics and Optical Modeling](15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md) by prioritizing surface material [decomposition](#7254-decomposition.md) and relighting over volumetric attenuation equations, although both families modify the core Gaussian properties beyond simple color [G].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family inherit the standard [3D Gaussian Splatting representation](#2257-3d-gaussian-splatting-3dgs-preliminaries.md) and rendering pipeline from [Scene Representation and Geometry Constraints](15421-scene-representation-and-geometry-constraints.md) [G]. The core variation across methods lies in the definition, storage, and optimization of $\mathbf{c}_i(\omega)$ and potentially $\alpha_i$, moving beyond the fixed [SH coefficients](#5603-spherical-harmonics.md) used in base 3DGS [G]. Common strategies include:
1.  **Post-Processing Transformation:** Applying a learned affine transformation to the rendered image based on 3D position and view embedding [G].
2.  **Factorized Illumination:** Separating scene lighting (via a tensor grid) from material properties (via [BRDF](#14809-bidirectional-reflectance-distribution-function-brdf.md) features) to model specular effects [G].
3.  **Image-Conditioned Modulation:** Using an MLP and per-image embeddings to modulate Gaussian color and opacity, enabling transient object removal and appearance synthesis [G].
4.  **Neural Field Substitution:** Replacing per-Gaussian SH with a shared grid-based neural field to reduce parameters and improve generalization [G].
5.  **Volumetric Attenuation:** Modifying the [alpha-blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md) equation to incorporate medium properties, such as direct attenuation $B_d$ and backscatter parameters $B_\infty, B_b$, to model light transport in non-vacuum media [G].

## Subtopics

### [Color and Appearance Modeling](14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md)
**What it is:** Extends the standard [3DGS representation](#12855-gaussian-representation-and-truncation.md) by replacing or augmenting the fixed Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients with more flexible mechanisms to represent view-dependent color, lighting, and material properties [G].
**What sets it apart:** Focuses on radiance and material representation rather than volumetric [light transport equations](#1194-radiative-transfer-equation-formulation.md) [G].
**When to choose:** When base 3DGS struggles with complex specularities, dynamic lighting variations, or transient objects in unstructured datasets [G].
**Link:** [Color and Appearance Modeling](14740-color-and-appearance-modeling.md)

### [Physics and Optical Modeling](15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md)
**What it is:** Extends the standard 3DGS representation to handle non-vacuum media and physically consistent [surface extraction](#29-surface-extraction.md) by modifying the rendering equation or the underlying density field [G].
**What sets it apart:** Explicitly models volumetric attenuation and backscatter or reformulates the Gaussian primitive as a continuous [attenuation field](#9639-attenuation-field.md), unlike surface-focused material decomposition [G].
**When to choose:** When modeling light transport [in scattering](#13241-in-scattering.md) media (e.g., underwater fog) or requiring geometric consistency for surface reconstruction [G].
**Link:** [Physics and Optical Modeling](15148-physics-and-optical-modeling.md)

### Relightable 3D Gaussians
**Definition**
[Relightable 3D Gaussians](#6001-relightable-3d-gaussian.md) is a differentiable [point-based rendering](#2827-point-based-rendering.md) framework that enhances vanilla 3D Gaussians by associating extra properties (normal vectors, BRDF parameters, and incident lighting) to achieve photo-realistic relighting and BRDF decomposition from multi-view images [S1].

**Implementation Steps**
1.  Assign a normal vector $\mathbf{n}$, BRDF values, and incident light information to each 3D Gaussian point to model per-point light reflectance [S1].
2.  Apply physically based rendering (PBR) to get a PBR color for each 3D Gaussian point, which is then alpha-composited to obtain the rendered color for the corresponding image pixel [S1].
3.  Split the incident light into a global environment map and an indirect incident light field for robust material and [lighting estimation](#19371-hybrid-lighting-prediction-network.md) [S1].
4.  Introduce proper regularizations to enhance geometry and mitigate material-lighting ambiguity, including constraints on depth distribution, [smoothness priors](#11408-smoothness-priors.md), and a lighting regularization [S1].

### GeoSplatting Loss Function
**Definition**
[GeoSplatting Loss Function](#10241-inverse-rendering-loss-function.md) is a [composite loss](#15617-composite-loss.md) function for end-to-end training of GeoSplatting, combining photometric loss, [entropy loss](#2114-entropy-loss.md), [smoothness regularization](#19019-smoothness-regularization.md), and [light regularization](#15253-light-regularization.md) [S2].

**Implementation Steps**
1.  Compute [L1 loss](#15480-normalized-l1-loss.md) and SSIM loss between rendered image and ground truth [S2].
2.  Compute object [mask loss](#12742-loss-masking.md) $L_{mask}$ (MSE between rendered alpha map and ground truth object mask) [S2].
3.  Add entropy loss $L_{entropy}$ to constrain the shape, following DMTet and [FlexiCubes](#3669-flexicubes.md) [S2].
4.  Apply smoothness regularization on $k_d$ and $k_s$, and light regularization, following NVdiffrecmc and R3DG [S2].

**Formula**
The photometric loss is computed as:
$$ L_{img} = L_1 + \lambda_{ssim} L_{SSIM} + \lambda_{mask} L_{mask} $$
where $L_{mask}$ is MSE between rendered alpha map and ground truth object mask [S2].

**Comparison**
Unlike vanilla 3DGS or other methods requiring dist loss or pseudo depth normal loss for geometric constraints, GeoSplatting does not require these regularization terms due to explicit geometry guidance [S2].

### Split-Sum Warm-up
**Definition**
Split-Sum Warm-up is a training initialization technique that uses the split-sum approximation to pre-compute lighting integrals during early training stages to mitigate optimization instability caused by noisy geometry [S2].

**Implementation Steps**
1.  During early training, use the split-sum approximation (Eq. 6) which enables fast [pre-computation](#2330-pre-computation.md) and enhances evaluation speed [S2].
2.  After the [warm-up stage](#18447-warm-up-stage.md), transition to Monte Carlo sampling of the full rendering equation (Eq. 2) to incorporate shadow effects and inter-reflection [S2].

**Formula**
The split-sum approximation assumes no self-occlusion and is defined as:
$$ L_o(\omega_o) \approx \left[ \int_{\mathcal{H}} f_r(\omega_i, \omega_o) |\mathbf{n} \cdot \omega_i| \, d\omega_i \right] \cdot \left[ \int_{\mathcal{H}} L_{dir}(\omega_i) D |\mathbf{n} \cdot \omega_i| \, d\omega_i \right] $$
[S2]

**Pitfall**
Directly evaluating the full integral in Eq. 2 is inefficient and may lead to optimization instability during initial training when geometry is noisy [S2]. Split-sum avoids this but lacks self-occlusion modeling, potentially baking shadows into albedo [S2].

## Background
Relightable 3D Gaussians was introduced by [Gao et al](#9230-n-dimensional-gaussian-6dgs-7dgs.md). in 2024, presenting a framework for photo-realistic relighting using BRDF decomposition and ray tracing [S1]. GeoSplatting was introduced by its authors in 2025, focusing on geometry-guided physically-based inverse rendering [S2]. These methods address the need for editable, physically plausible scene representations in computer graphics and vision applications, moving beyond static appearance capture [G].

## Sources
